title: Root condition
hookLine: greed, hate, delusion, and their opposites as roots that hold a moment up

lines: THE LIST STARTS WITH THE ROOT.
cards: After a big storm, some trees are down across the road and some are still standing, bent but fine. Walk up to a fallen one and sometimes the reason is lying right there: a shallow plate of roots torn out of the ground.
Whatever a tree looks like above the soil, what keeps it upright is what's underneath. The Patthana opens its list of twenty-four conditions in the same place.
Before object, before support, before kamma, it starts with the root.

teach.b: The Pali is hetu paccaya, the root condition. The Abhidhamma names six roots. Three are unwholesome: greed, hatred and delusion.
Three are wholesome: non-greed, which shows up as generosity; non-hatred, which shows up as kindness; and non-delusion, which is wisdom.

In the suttas, the Buddha had already called greed, hatred and delusion the roots of what is unwholesome, and said that whatever a person does from them leads to suffering. The Patthana adds the mechanics.

teach.h: A ROOT HOLDS A MOMENT FIRM.
teach.b: A root conditions the moment it sits in by holding it firm.
The commentators reach for a tree too: as roots give a tree its footing, a root gives a mind-moment its stability and direction. A moment of anger rooted in hatred grips hard.
A moment of giving rooted in non-greed stands steady too. And not every moment has a root.
In the manual, bare seeing, bare hearing, the simple receiving of an object, are rootless moments: they happen and pass without greed or kindness in them.
The roots come in later, with the javana moments where the mind takes a side. So a sound at the window isn't greedy or hateful. What grows from it might be.
When an act surprises you, your own or someone else's, the root question is simple: what was holding this up? Wanting? Pushing away?
Not seeing clearly? Or the other three: letting go, goodwill, understanding. The surface of a tree can fool you.
The roots tell you how it will stand in the wind.

how: Abhidhamma students learn the root condition first among the Patthana's conditions, and some Theravada teachers invite reflection on whether an act came from greed, hatred and delusion or from generosity, kindness and wisdom.

o: the root under a moment that holds it firm
the habit a past life leaves in this one
the first cause that set the world in motion

games.q: the six roots: tap the pairs.

s: every moment of mind has a root
in the manual, bare seeing, hearing and receiving are rootless; roots come in with the moments that take a side.
the Abhidhamma names six roots, three wholesome and three unwholesome
greed, hatred, delusion, and non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion.
the root condition comes first in the Patthana's list
before object, before support, before kamma.

games.q: a car alarm goes off outside your window. by the manual's account, is the bare hearing of it greedy or hateful?
o: neither: bare hearing has no root
greedy: you want it to stop
games.why: bare hearing is a rootless moment. what grows from it, in the javana moments, may be rooted in aversion, or in patience.

practice: Bring to mind one small thing you did today, making coffee, sending a message, holding a door, and look at it the way you'd look at the base of a tree: what was underneath?
Wanting something, avoiding something, care for someone, maybe more than one; don't judge what you find, just name it. Then let the act go, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Root condition. The first of the twenty-four: greed, hatred, delusion, or their three opposites, holding a moment firm the way roots hold a tree. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: root, cause; in the Patthana, the first condition, the six roots that hold a moment firm.

carryVoice: Your line: roots hold it up. Six roots: three that trouble a moment, three that steady it. That's today, done.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.69 (Akusalamula Sutta), the roots of the unwholesome
